turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I... I guess I came in because I keep doing these odd things at church lately. 

Like, we have a potluck on Sundays. Sister Mary always brings her macaroni salad, though she puts way too much celery in it if you ask me. I used to grow celery when we had the house out on County Road 9, but the soil out there was always too sandy for a good garden. The tomatoes did alright, though. 

Anyway, I was standing by the potluck table, and I picked up the big serving spoon for the potatoes, and I just... held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and not moving at all. Just froze right there. 

And then later, I was at the end of the table with the napkins. They were those yellow paper ones. Yellow is such a happy color, it reminds me of the kitchen curtains I bought at Sears back when they still mailed out that big thick catalog... I really miss getting that catalog in the mail. But I was folding the same stack of napkins, just folding them over and over, smoothing them down and folding them again, and all those people were just standing there in line waiting on me to finish so they could get their silverware. I don't really know why I get stuck like that.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off-topic about growing celery, sandy soil, and Sears catalogs before returning to the main point.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing in place holding a spoon (posturing/catalepsy) and repetitively folding napkins (stereotypy).

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is there?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just the regular sounds, you know? Like the wind chimes on my porch. I have these beautiful glass ones my sister got me when she went down to Florida. Clearwater, I think it was. Or maybe Daytona? She always loved the beach, but I could never stand the sand getting in my shoes. It just ruins a good pair of loafers. I used to have a pair of penny loafers that I wore until the soles practically fell off. They were so comfortable, like walking on clouds. But no... no voices. Just the wind chimes.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits tangentiality, wandering from wind chimes to Florida, beaches, sand, and penny loafers before returning to the topic.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices when no one is there.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times lately when you felt unusually energetic or excited for days at a time?
turns.patient_response: Energetic? Oh, heavens no. I don't think I've had that kind of energy since... well, since I was a girl. I remember one summer, I must have been about twelve, and we were staying at my aunt's farm. She had these big, beautiful draft horses. Clydesdales, they were. Such gentle giants, you know? They had those big feathery hooves. I used to brush their coats until they shone like copper pennies. Pennies used to buy you a whole handful of candy down at the mercantile. Peppermint sticks, licorice whips... I always liked the butterscotch discs the best. They came in those little shiny yellow wrappers. So pretty. But no, I wouldn't say I've felt unusually excited or anything like that lately. Just my normal self, I suppose.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits loose associations and circumstantiality, drifting from the topic of energy to childhood memories of horses, pennies, and candy before finally returning to answer the question.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies feeling unusually excited lately.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having unusual energy, stating she hasn't felt that kind of energy since she was a girl.

turns.doctor_question: Since you were a child, have social situations usually felt confusing to you?
turns.patient_response: Confusing? Oh, I don't know... I've always just been me, you know? I remember when I first started school, it was a little one-room schoolhouse out past the old mill. The teacher, Miss Gable, she had the most beautiful handwriting. Perfect cursive, all those loops and swirls. We used to practice on these little slate boards with chalk that always made my hands feel so dry. I hate that feeling, dry hands. I use this rosewater lotion now, comes in a pink bottle. Smells just like the roses my grandmother grew on her trellis. They were those big climbing roses, the kind that bloom all summer long... But no, I wouldn't say confusing. Just... normal, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the question about social situations to unrelated topics like a teacher's handwriting, chalk, lotion, and roses.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any recent medical illness or brain problem, like a seizure, stroke, or head injury?
turns.patient_response: A stroke or a head injury? Oh, goodness no. My head is perfectly fine. I haven't been sick or in a hospital since... well, since my Henry broke his collarbone. That was years and years ago. He was up fixing the roof on that old shed out back. It had those green shingles, you know? The kind that get all thick with moss if you don't scrape them down in the spring. I told him to hire someone to do it, but he was always so stubborn about fixing things himself. Just like his father. His father used to smoke this pipe that smelled just like sweet cherry wood. It would fill up the whole porch. Smelled a bit like cherry pie, actually. I love a good cherry pie, especially if you make the crust from scratch and do the lattice on top. You have to weave the dough strips just right or they sink right down into the fruit while it bakes... But no, no seizures or anything like that for me. Just healthy, I suppose.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from a question about head injuries to a broken collarbone, roof shingles, moss, a smoking pipe, and baking a cherry pie.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe anyone is trying to harm you or control you?
turns.patient_response: Harm me? Oh, heavens no. Why would anyone want to do that? I keep to myself mostly, just me and my little garden out back. I've been trying to get the tomatoes to come in, but the squirrels keep getting to them before they turn red. They're such clever little things, squirrels. They have those bushy tails that twitch when they're excited. I used to watch them chase each other up and down the big oak tree we had in the front yard when I was a girl. That tree must have been a hundred years old. My brother built a treehouse up in the branches. We'd sit up there for hours and eat sandwiches... egg salad, usually. Mother always put a little bit of paprika in her egg salad, gave it such a nice color. I still have her old recipe box, it's made of tin with little painted daisies on the lid. But no, nobody's trying to control me or anything like that. I'm just fine.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, wandering extensively from the initial question to topics about gardening, squirrels, childhood memories, and egg salad.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having any beliefs that someone is trying to harm or control her.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever find yourself repeating other people’s words right after they say them?
turns.patient_response: Repeating words? No, I don't think I do that. It sounds a bit like an echo, doesn't it? Like when you stand at the edge of a canyon and shout down into it. We went to the Grand Canyon once, Henry and I, for our twenty-fifth anniversary. It was so hot that day, the sun just beating down on the rocks. The rocks were all these different shades of red and orange, like a painting. I bought a little postcard from the gift shop with a picture of a mule on it. They take people down into the canyon on mules, you know. I'd never ride one, though. Mules can be so stubborn. My uncle Arthur had a mule on his farm back when I was little. He called him Barnaby. Barnaby loved to eat carrots right out of your hand, but you had to keep your fingers flat or he'd nip you. I was always so careful with my hands around him... But no, I don't go around repeating what people say.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from the topic of repeating words to echoes, the Grand Canyon, mules, and a childhood memory of an uncle's farm.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies repeating other people's words, which rules out the echolalia subtype of disorganized behavior.

turns.doctor_question: As a child, did you often do the same movement or routine over and over again?
turns.patient_response: Over and over? No, I don't recall doing anything like that. I was just a regular little girl, mostly just running around outside. We did play jump rope a lot, I suppose, if that counts? You have to jump the exact same way every time or the rope catches your ankles. My friend Martha and I would jump rope for hours on the sidewalk until the streetlights came on. Martha had the most beautiful blonde hair, always tied up in two braids with little red ribbons. Her mother made those ribbons from scraps of velvet. Velvet is such a difficult fabric to sew, you know. It slips all over the machine if you aren't careful. I tried making a velvet dress for my baby doll once, but the needle kept jamming. It was a Singer sewing machine, one of those heavy black iron ones with the gold filigree painted on the side. My mother bought it second-hand from a lady down the street who was moving up to Chicago. Chicago always sounded so windy and cold to me, all those tall buildings blocking out the sun... I've never been, myself. But no, no strange routines or movements for me. Just regular playing.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from jump rope to a friend's hair, velvet ribbons, sewing machines, and the city of Chicago.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies having any strange movements or routines as a child, ruling out stereotypies or mannerisms.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient denies engaging in any repetitive routines or movements over and over again.

turns.doctor_question: When someone tries to move your arms or body while you’re frozen, do you stay in that position?
turns.patient_response: Frozen? Oh, goodness, no. I don't freeze up like a statue or anything. And who would be trying to move my arms anyway? It's just me here. The only thing frozen around here is the ground beef I put in the icebox. I always buy the big family pack when it goes on sale at the market. You have to remember to separate it into little portions before you freeze it, though, or it takes absolutely forever to thaw out on the counter. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she just throws the whole big block right into her freezer, paper and all. Then she complains when she can't get her meatloaf made in time for supper. She makes a terribly dry meatloaf anyway, puts way too much onion in it. Onions give me such awful heartburn. I always have to drink a little glass of milk with a spoonful of baking soda stirred in if I have onions. My grandmother taught me that trick. She lived to be ninety-two, bless her heart, and she swore by baking soda for just about everything... But no, I move my own arms just fine. Nobody is posing me like a mannequin.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of being physically frozen to frozen ground beef, meatloaf, onions, heartburn, and her grandmother.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies freezing up like a statue or having her arms posed by others, rejecting symptoms of catalepsy or waxy flexibility.

turns.doctor_question: When you get stuck like that, do you stop talking too?
turns.patient_response: Stuck? Well, like I just said, I don't get frozen or stuck in the first place. And I certainly don't stop talking. My husband Henry, God rest his soul, he always used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey. He had all these funny little sayings like that. His father was in the Merchant Marines, you see, so Henry picked up all sorts of phrases from him. He had this beautiful old compass his father brought back from a trip... maybe it was Nova Scotia? It was solid brass and just so heavy. I used to have to polish it every Sunday before church with that stinky Brasso cream. It always left a terrible black smudge on my good dusting rags. I tried soaking them in bleach, but you have to be so careful with bleach or it eats right through the cotton. I ruined one of my favorite aprons that way, a lovely little yellow gingham one with pockets on the front. I used to keep my clothespins in those pockets when I hung the wash out on the line... But no, I don't stop talking or get stuck like you're saying.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient states she 'certainly doesn't stop talking' and provides a lengthy, verbose response.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, drifting from the topic of talking to her husband, a brass compass, polishing, bleach, and an apron before returning to the question.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies getting 'frozen or stuck' and denies stopping talking (mutism).

turns.doctor_question: Do people ever tell you that your talking jumps from one idea to another in a way that’s hard to follow?
turns.patient_response: Well, I suppose sometimes folks do look a bit confused when I'm talking. Like at the church, when the ladies ask me about the new blankets for the bazaar or what time choir practice is. I always mean to give them a straight answer, I really do. But then I start talking, and my words just sort of run off on their own... I'll start talking about the green beans I'm canning, and then that reminds me of a hymn we sang last Easter, and before I know it I'm going on about how my yellow roses are doing this year. And they just stare at me, like they can't quite find what I'm saying in all of that. My roses really are lovely this year, though. I put down some crushed eggshells around the roots, just like my mother used to do. She always saved her eggshells in a little tin cup on the windowsill. It was a blue tin cup, the kind that had those little white speckles all over it. We used to take those cups camping when I was a little girl... but yes, I suppose people do have a hard time following me sometimes.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient confirms that her speech jumps from one unrelated topic to another (e.g., from blankets to green beans to hymns to roses) and that others have a hard time following her, demonstrating disorganized thinking and speech (tangentiality/derailment).

turns.doctor_question: About how long have your speech and these getting-stuck episodes been going on?
turns.patient_response: Well, let me think... I'd say it's been about six months now that folks have been mentioning my talking being hard to follow, and noticing me acting a bit odd. Six months... that would mean it started right around the time of the big autumn bake sale at the church. I remember because I made three dozen of my special molasses cookies. You have to use the real dark molasses, none of that light stuff, or they just don't taste right. And a pinch of ginger, that's the secret. My sister Edna, she always tried to make them, but hers always came out flat as a pancake. She never did have the touch for baking, Edna. She was better with sewing. She made me the most beautiful quilt for my wedding, all done in the double wedding ring pattern. It had these lovely little scraps of calico fabric... I think some of them were from our old dresses when we were girls. I still have it folded up at the bottom of my cedar chest. Cedar smells so wonderful, doesn't it? It keeps the moths away, too. I always put a few cedar blocks in with my winter coats when I pack them up for the summer... but yes, it's been about six months since all this started.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient notes that others find her talking 'hard to follow' and demonstrates tangential speech by wandering off-topic about cookies, her sister, and cedar chests before answering the question.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms the doctor's reference to 'getting-stuck episodes' by acknowledging she has been 'acting a bit odd' for the past six months.
